system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2167-08-06 14:52:00 to 2167-08-08 16:24:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A young woman with a history of tracheobronchomalacia and chronic tracheostomy was admitted for worsening odynophagia, green sputum, chest and throat pain, and dyspnea on exertion. She had recently completed a course of doxycycline for suspected MRSA tracheitis. On admission, she was afebrile with stable vitals and no radiographic abnormalities. Labs showed mild anemia but no leukocytosis. A deep tracheal sputum culture confirmed MRSA, and she was treated with a 7-day course of intravenous vancomycin. A CT neck showed no new inflammatory changes or fluid collection. A bedside swallow evaluation indicated mild oropharyngeal dysphagia without aspiration risk. Her symptoms improved, and she was transitioned to oral intake. Her tracheostomy tube was replaced after antibiotic completion as part of MRSA decolonization. She was discharged home with lidocaine for throat pain and instructions for home hygiene, with follow-up planned with infectious disease and pulmonary specialists.
problems: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia originating in the perinatal period
Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection as the cause of diseases classified elsewhere

diagnoses.long_title: Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified
Carrier or suspected carrier of Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve been having a lot of pain when I swallow. It started a week ago and got worse fast. Two days ago, I couldn’t swallow at all without feeling like I was choking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Where does it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: From under my chin down to my chest. It’s sharp, and it’s there even when I’m not swallowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And any fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever, but I’ve had chills and felt cold the past two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any cough or sputum?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thick yellow sputum from my trach, and it smells bad. I saw a little blood in it two days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I remember you were just discharged last week for a similar issue—MRSA tracheitis. You finished vancomycin, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I finished it. My sputum cleared up for a couple of days, but then it came back and got worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you haven’t been able to eat or drink at all in the last two days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing. I tried, but it just hurts too much. I haven’t taken my pills either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help with the pain. You got some IV Dilaudid in the ER. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still bad. I need something stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stick to your home pain plan—liquid Tylenol and oxycodone as needed. We also have lidocaine gel you can swish to numb the throat before trying to drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I’m scared I’ll never be able to eat again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve checked your trach site—it looks clean, no infection signs. Your chest X-ray and neck X-ray are normal too. No pneumonia or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely related to your tracheitis flaring up again. Your trach is colonized with MRSA, so it can cause irritation even without a full infection. The dysphagia seems oropharyngeal—your GI and ENT doctors don’t think it’s in the esophagus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I just had antibiotics for that. Why is it back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because MRSA is living in your trach. It’s not a new infection, so we’re not restarting antibiotics. We’ll treat the symptoms—pain, nausea, and help you start drinking again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your labs came back. Your white count is normal, which supports that this isn’t a new infection. Your hemoglobin is low, but it’s been that way before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no more IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not this time. Your body isn’t showing signs of fighting an infection. We’ll keep focusing on symptom relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I tried some apple juice with the lidocaine and got it down without choking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’ll keep encouraging small sips of thin liquids. Try crushing your pills in applesauce when you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the green sputum?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s from the chronic MRSA colonization. As long as you don’t have fever or worsening pain, it’s not a concern. Keep using the saline nebs through your trach to loosen secretions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nursing team says you had a small episode of regurgitation last night. Did it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was uncomfortable, but not as painful. I think I just drank too fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Take it slow. We’re not worried—your vitals are stable, and you’re not dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been thinking—could my depression be making this worse? I’ve been stressed about moving out and managing everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a really good point. Chronic pain and illness can take a toll. We’ll keep you on your fluoxetine and suggest seeing a therapist for support and coping strategies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve tolerated liquids and soft foods, and your pain is better controlled. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What should I do if this happens again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stick to thin liquids and soft solids. Crush pills in applesauce. Use lidocaine before eating. If you get green sputum or trach pain, try Tylenol and lidocaine first. If you develop fever or trouble breathing, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I still can’t swallow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your GI doctor. They might repeat a swallow study. We also recommend seeing a nutritionist to make sure you’re getting enough calories.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send you home with ondansetron for nausea, and all your usual meds. Keep up with your trach care and oral hygiene three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel a lot better knowing what to do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’re here if you need us.

summary.summary_paragraph: A young woman with a history of tracheobronchomalacia and chronic tracheostomy was admitted for worsening odynophagia and dysphagia, two days after being unable to swallow without choking. She had recently completed a course of vancomycin for MRSA tracheitis, but symptoms recurred with thick, foul-smelling sputum from her trach. She remained afebrile with stable vital signs and no leukocytosis. Imaging showed no acute abnormalities in the chest or neck. ENT and GI evaluations found no structural or esophageal cause for dysphagia. She was treated symptomatically with pain management, dietary modifications, and anti-nausea medication. She gradually tolerated oral intake and was discharged home with instructions for ongoing symptom management, follow-up with GI and mental health providers, and reinforcement of trach and oral care.
